turns.text: Free public transport gets cars off the road and helps people who cannot afford fares. When Tallinn made buses free for residents in 2013, ridership rose, and the city kept the system running for over a decade.

Tallinn’s experiment is less persuasive than claimed: many new riders were existing drivers who simply shifted, while the city had to replace fare revenue with general taxes, crowding out other services. That is my first point—free transport is not free; someone pays, and flat subsidies often favor wealthier commuters over the poor. Second, free fares remove the price signal that manages crowding. When Luxembourg made all transit free in 2020, overcrowding on busy lines worsened and operators struggled to add capacity. Better policy targets affordability directly with discounted passes, keeping fares to fund reliable service where it matters most.

My opponent says fares fund the system, but fares cover only part of running costs in most cities; the rest is already public money. Removing fares also removes ticket machines, inspectors and boarding delays.

My opponent says fares cover only part of costs, but that partial revenue is still real money: eliminating it forces cuts, higher taxes, or both, and the savings from ticket machines and inspectors are small next to the loss. Removing boarding delays also cuts both ways—without any barrier, systems attract non-essential trips and fare evasion becomes harder to manage, so crowding and cost creep upward. My case stands: flat free fares are a blunt subsidy that often helps wealthier commuters more than the poor. Targeted discounts for low-income riders protect affordability while keeping fare revenue to maintain reliable service where it is needed most. That is smarter than making everything free.

The other side never showed that fares, rather than funding choices, keep buses running. Free transport widens access, cuts traffic and costs less than its critics claim. That is why the motion should pass.

The PRO side never answered the core clash: free transport is not free. Eliminating fares means losing real revenue, which forces tax increases, service cuts, or both. They also failed to address that flat free fares are a blunt subsidy, often benefiting wealthier commuters more than the poor. Meanwhile, my side showed that targeted discounts protect affordability while preserving fare revenue for reliable service. The claim that free transit widens access ignores the crowding and cost creep we highlighted. We won the debate because we offered a smarter, targeted solution, while they relied on wishful thinking about cost-free universal free rides. That is why the motion should fail.

scorecard.summary: CON wins the debate because they directly addressed the funding, equity, and crowding objections while offering a targeted alternative, whereas PRO left the central 'not free' and distributional critiques largely unanswered. CON's structured use of multiple examples and point-by-point rebuttals made their case more persuasive on the written record.
